clinicalPearls: Hepatoerythropoietic porphyria is the rare biallelic (homozygous or compound heterozygous) form of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency — effectively the severe childhood counterpart of familial porphyria cutanea tarda.

It usually presents in infancy or early childhood with marked blistering photosensitivity, skin fragility, scarring, hypertrichosis and often reddish or dark urine that may fluoresce under ultraviolet light.
The clinical picture overlaps congenital erythropoietic porphyria (Gunther disease), so severe childhood blistering porphyria must be worked up carefully to distinguish the two.

Because uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase is deficient in both liver and erythroid tissue, patients characteristically show raised erythrocyte zinc-protoporphyrin in addition to the uroporphyrin and heptacarboxyl-porphyrin excess seen in porphyria cutanea tarda.
Urinary porphyrins are dominated by uroporphyrin and heptacarboxylate porphyrin, while faecal isocoproporphyrin — the hallmark of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase block — is also increased.
Enzyme activity is grossly reduced (typically only a small residual fraction), far lower than the roughly half-normal activity in familial porphyria cutanea tarda carriers.
Some patients develop haemolytic anaemia with splenomegaly, and iron overload can aggravate the cutaneous disease, so iron status and haematological indices should be assessed.

There is no specific cure; management is lifelong rigorous photoprotection, avoidance of skin trauma and aggravating factors (iron overload, alcohol, oestrogens), and supportive care, since the phlebotomy and low-dose antimalarial approaches used in porphyria cutanea tarda are far less effective here.
reference.pathophysiology: Hepatoerythropoietic porphyria results from inheritance of pathogenic variants in UROD on both alleles, producing a profound deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, the fifth enzyme of haem biosynthesis, which sequentially removes the four carboxyl groups from uroporphyrinogen III to yield coproporphyrinogen III. When enzyme activity falls to a small residual fraction, partially decarboxylated intermediates accumulate, notably uroporphyrinogen and heptacarboxyl-porphyrinogen, and an aberrant side reaction generates isocoproporphyrin that is excreted in faeces as a diagnostic marker. Unlike sporadic and familial porphyria cutanea tarda, where a single defective allele or acquired hepatic enzyme inhibition suffices, hepatoerythropoietic porphyria reflects near-complete constitutional loss of the enzyme across tissues, so the porphyrin excess is present in erythroid precursors as well as the liver — hence the raised erythrocyte zinc-protoporphyrin and the tendency to haemolysis and splenomegaly. Accumulated porphyrins are potent photosensitisers: on absorbing visible light they generate reactive oxygen species in the skin, producing subepidermal blistering, fragility, scarring, milia and hypertrichosis on light-exposed areas. Hepatic iron accumulation and oxidative stress further inhibit residual enzyme activity, and factors that worsen porphyria cutanea tarda — iron overload, alcohol, oestrogens, hepatitis and sun exposure — can likewise aggravate the phenotype. The severity broadly correlates with how little functional enzyme the particular genotype leaves intact.

additionalInvestigations: Urinary porphyrin fractionation showing predominant uroporphyrin and heptacarboxyl-porphyrin
Faecal porphyrin analysis demonstrating raised isocoproporphyrin
Erythrocyte porphyrins including a raised zinc-protoporphyrin fraction
Plasma porphyrin fluorescence scan for confirmation and to distinguish from other porphyrias
UROD molecular genetic testing for biallelic variants
Full blood count, reticulocytes and iron studies to assess haemolysis and iron overload
redFlags: Severe blistering and mutilating scarring with secondary infection in a young child
Evidence of significant iron overload or deteriorating liver function
Corneal or ocular involvement from photosensitivity and scarring
Rapidly worsening skin fragility after a new aggravating exposure
reference.prognosis: Hepatoerythropoietic porphyria is a chronic lifelong disorder whose severity tracks the degree of residual enzyme activity, ranging from disfiguring scarring and functional impairment to comparatively milder disease; strict photoprotection and avoidance of aggravating factors limit cutaneous damage. Life expectancy is usually preserved, but severe cases carry substantial morbidity from scarring, anaemia and iron-related complications.
pitfalls: Confusing it with congenital erythropoietic porphyria, since both cause severe childhood blistering photosensitivity
Treating it as ordinary porphyria cutanea tarda and expecting a good response to phlebotomy or low-dose antimalarials
Overlooking the raised erythrocyte zinc-protoporphyrin that signals the erythroid component of the enzyme defect
Missing coexisting haemolysis, splenomegaly or iron overload that modify management
Failing to counsel on lifelong photoprotection and avoidance of iron, alcohol and oestrogen triggers

management: Strict lifelong photoprotection is the mainstay: opaque physical sunblocks, tightly woven protective clothing, gloves and window filters against visible and long-wave ultraviolet light
Avoid aggravating factors that increase porphyrin load, including alcohol, oestrogens, iron overload and hepatotoxic drugs
Attempt reduction of hepatic porphyrin burden with cautious phlebotomy or low-dose antimalarials such as hydroxychloroquine, recognising the limited response given near-complete enzyme deficiency
Meticulous skin care with gentle wound management of blisters and erosions, prompt treatment of secondary infection and avoidance of friction and minor trauma to fragile skin
Serial monitoring of urinary, faecal and erythrocyte porphyrins, iron studies and liver function, with surveillance for hepatic complications
Multidisciplinary care coordinated between a specialist porphyria centre, dermatology and paediatrics
Genetic counselling and cascade family screening for biallelic UROD variants
